statement: Let $A$ be a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) over a field $k$, $B$ a [normal Hopf subalgebra](c:normal-sub-hopf-algebra), and $A$ [flat](c:flat-module) as a right $B$-module. For a $B$-module $M$ and an $A$-module $N$, the [Ext groups](c:ext-group) satisfy $\operatorname{Ext}^n_A(A\otimes_B M, N) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_B(M, N)$ for all $n \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a [Hopf algebra](c:hopf-algebra) over a field $k$.
$M$ is a left $B$-module and $N$ is a left $A$-module, which is a $B$-module by restriction.

conclusion: There is an isomorphism $\operatorname{Ext}^n_A(A\otimes_B M, N) \cong \operatorname{Ext}^n_B(M, N)$ for every $n \ge 0$, natural in $M$ and $N$.

proofs.name: Induced projective resolution
proofs.slogan: Induce a projective resolution of $M$ from $B$ to $A$, then match the two Hom complexes by adjunction.
proofs.scope: The whole isomorphism. The proof uses only flatness of $A$ over $B$; the Hopf structure and normality are not needed, and other forms of the change of rings theorem (for comodules, with the quotient $A//B$) are not proved here.

roles.why: Only the ring structure of $A$ is used here; the coproduct and antipode play no part.
Normality gives the quotient Hopf algebra $A//B$ for other forms of the theorem, not for this isomorphism.
Flatness of $A$ over $B$ makes induction exact, so the induced complex is still a resolution.
The resolution is built for $M$, and $N$ is the coefficient module of both Hom complexes.

steps.slogan: Choose a projective resolution of $M$ over $B$.
steps.detail: Let $P_\bullet \to M$ be a [projective resolution](c:has-projective-resolution) by projective left $B$-modules. It exists because every module has one. Then $\operatorname{Ext}^n_B(M,N) = H^n(\operatorname{Hom}_B(P_\bullet, N))$.

steps.slogan: Apply $A \otimes_B -$ to get a complex of projective $A$-modules.
steps.detail: The module $A \otimes_B B = A$ is free over $A$. The functor $A\otimes_B -$ keeps direct sums and direct summands, so each $A \otimes_B P_i$ is a projective $A$-module.

steps.slogan: Use flatness to show that the induced complex is still a resolution.
steps.detail: Because $A$ is [flat](c:flat-module) as a right $B$-module, $A \otimes_B -$ is exact. So $A\otimes_B P_\bullet \to A \otimes_B M$ is exact, and with the last step it is a projective resolution over $A$.

steps.slogan: Match $A$-linear maps out of the induced modules with $B$-linear maps.
steps.detail: Extension and restriction of scalars are adjoint: $\operatorname{Hom}_A(A\otimes_B P, N) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_B(P, N)$, naturally in $P$. So the complexes $\operatorname{Hom}_A(A\otimes_B P_\bullet, N)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_B(P_\bullet, N)$ are isomorphic.

steps.slogan: Take cohomology of the two isomorphic Hom complexes.
steps.detail: By the resolution of the last steps, $\operatorname{Ext}^n_A(A\otimes_B M, N) = H^n(\operatorname{Hom}_A(A\otimes_B P_\bullet, N)) \cong H^n(\operatorname{Hom}_B(P_\bullet, N)) = \operatorname{Ext}^n_B(M,N)$, and the maps are natural.

concepts.c:hopf-algebra: The theorem is stated for Hopf algebras, but the proof uses only the algebra structure.
concepts.c:normal-sub-hopf-algebra: Normality is part of the setting; this proof does not use it.
concepts.c:flat-module: Flatness makes induction from $B$ to $A$ exact.
concepts.c:ext-group: The Ext groups are the cohomology of the Hom complexes.
concepts.c:has-projective-resolution: A projective resolution of $M$ computes the Ext groups over $B$ and, after induction, over $A$.

source.note: The Eckmann-Shapiro lemma for the ring map $B \to A$, as in Weibel, An Introduction to Homological Algebra (1994). Flatness holds for connected graded Hopf algebras (Milnor and Moore, 1965) and finite dimensional ones (Nichols and Zoeller, 1989).

statement: In a [tetrahedron](c:tetrahedron) the four medians meet in one point $G$, and $G$ divides each median in the ratio $3:1$ counted from the vertex. A median joins a vertex to the [centroid](c:centroid) of the opposite face.

hypotheses.text: The points $A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3$ are the vertices of a [tetrahedron](c:tetrahedron) in real space.

conclusion: The medians $A_iF_i$ all pass through $G = \tfrac14(A_0 + A_1 + A_2 + A_3)$, and $\overrightarrow{A_iG} = 3\,\overrightarrow{GF_i}$ for each $i$, where $F_i$ is the [centroid](c:centroid) of the face opposite $A_i$.

formal.difference: The declaration is the vector identity $A_i - G = n\,(G - F_i)$ for an $n$-simplex over a division ring of characteristic zero; the tetrahedron is the case $n = 3$. Concurrence of the four medians follows because $G$ does not depend on $i$.

proofs.name: Averages of vectors from a vertex
proofs.slogan: Write both centroids as averages of vectors from the vertex $A_i$, and compare the two vectors.
proofs.scope: The case $n = 3$ of the simplex identity; the same computation gives the factor $n$ for an $n$-simplex. The proof treats points as vectors from a fixed origin, so it needs no coordinates.

roles.why: Four vertices make $G$ an average of four points and $F_i$ an average of three points.

steps.slogan: Define the centroid $G$ and the face centroid $F_i$ as equal-weight averages.
steps.detail: Put $G = \tfrac14 \sum_{x=0}^{3} A_x$ and $F_i = \tfrac13 \sum_{x \ne i} A_x$. In each case the weights add to $1$, so both points are [centroids](c:centroid) of vertices of the tetrahedron.

steps.slogan: Write the vector from $A_i$ to $F_i$ as one third of a sum.
steps.detail: Let $S_i = \sum_{x=0}^{3} (A_x - A_i)$, a sum of [vectors](c:vector) from $A_i$ to the four vertices; the term $x = i$ is zero. Then $F_i - A_i = \tfrac13 \sum_{x \ne i} (A_x - A_i) = \tfrac13 S_i$.

steps.slogan: Write the vector from $A_i$ to $G$ as one quarter of the same sum.
steps.detail: In the same way $G - A_i = \tfrac14 \sum_{x=0}^{3} (A_x - A_i) = \tfrac14 S_i$, because the four weights $\tfrac14$ add to $1$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two vectors to relate $G - F_i$ to $A_i - G$.
steps.detail: Then $G - F_i = (G - A_i) - (F_i - A_i) = (\tfrac14 - \tfrac13) S_i = -\tfrac1{12} S_i$. Also $A_i - G = -\tfrac14 S_i$. Hence $A_i - G = 3\,(G - F_i)$.

steps.slogan: Read off the ratio $3:1$ and note that $G$ does not depend on $i$.
steps.detail: The identity says that $G$ lies on the median $A_iF_i$ with $A_iG : GF_i = 3 : 1$. The point $G$ is the same for $i = 0, 1, 2, 3$, so all four medians pass through it.

concepts.c:tetrahedron: The four vertices of the tetrahedron are the points that the averages use.
concepts.c:centroid: Both $G$ and $F_i$ are centroids, that is, equal-weight averages of vertices.
concepts.c:vector: Subtracting points gives vectors from $A_i$, which makes the weights comparable.

source.note: mathlib rewrites the face centroid with faceOppositeCentroid_vsub_point_eq_smul_sum_vsub and the centroid with centroid_vsub_eq, then collects the coefficients with sub_smul and mul_inv_cancel₀.

statement: Let $0 < \varepsilon < \pi/2$. Let each $b_n$ be $0$ or a complex number with $|\arg b_n| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$, and let $b_1 \ne 0$. Then the [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction) $\mathbf{K}(1/b_n) = 1/(b_1 + 1/(b_2 + \cdots))$ [converges](c:convergence) if and only if $\sum_n |b_n|$ diverges.

hypotheses.text: Every partial denominator $b_n$ is $0$ or lies in the sector $|\arg b_n| \le \pi/2 - \varepsilon$, for a fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.
The first partial denominator $b_1$ is not zero.

proofs.name: Divergence by Stern-Stolz, convergence by sector bounds
proofs.slogan: A summable sequence makes even and odd approximants differ, and the sector bounds make the approximants converge otherwise.
proofs.scope: An outline: the direction from convergence to $\sum|b_n| = \infty$ is proved in full, and the converse rests on the cited work. All partial numerators equal $1$.

roles.why: The sector keeps the ratios $B_{n-1}/B_n$ in a sector and gives a lower bound for $|B_n|$.
The condition $b_1 \ne 0$ gives $B_1 \ne 0$ and starts the induction of the sector step.

steps.slogan: Write the approximants through a three-term recurrence.
steps.detail: The $n$th approximant is $S_n = A_n/B_n$ with $B_n = b_nB_{n-1} + B_{n-2}$, $B_{-1} = 0$, $B_0 = 1$, and the same recurrence for $A_n$ with $A_{-1} = 1$, $A_0 = 0$. The determinant identity $A_nB_{n-1} - A_{n-1}B_n = (-1)^{n-1}$ gives $S_n - S_{n-1} = (-1)^{n-1}/(B_nB_{n-1})$.

steps.slogan: Prove divergence when the series $\sum |b_n|$ converges.
steps.detail: Then $|A_n|$ and $|B_n|$ stay bounded by $\prod (1 + |b_k|)$. The differences $B_n - B_{n-2} = b_nB_{n-1}$ are summable, so the even and odd terms of $(A_n, B_n)$ converge to $(A_e, B_e)$ and $(A_o, B_o)$. The determinant identity gives $A_eB_o - A_oB_e = -1$, so the even and odd limits of $S_n$ differ.

steps.slogan: Keep the tail ratios $B_{n-1}/B_n$ inside the sector.
steps.detail: Put $f_n = B_{n-1}/B_n$, so that $f_n = 1/(b_n + f_{n-1})$ and $f_0 = 0$. The sector is closed under sums and inverses, so every $f_n$ lies in it, $B_n \ne 0$, and $|B_n| \ge \sin\varepsilon\,(|b_n||B_{n-1}| + |B_{n-2}|)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the approximants converge when $\sum |b_n|$ diverges.
steps.detail: This is the hard direction of the theorem. The cited proof uses the sector bounds of the last step to show that $(S_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence). The estimate is long, so it is cited and not repeated here.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: The finite-sum step shows that convergence forces $\sum |b_n| = \infty$. The infinite-sum step shows the converse. So $\mathbf{K}(1/b_n)$ converges if and only if $\sum |b_n|$ diverges.

concepts.c:continued-fraction: The approximants of the continued fraction are the sequence whose convergence is decided.
concepts.c:convergence: Convergence means that the approximants $S_n$ tend to a limit.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The hard direction shows that the approximants form a Cauchy sequence.

source.ref: E. B. Van Vleck, On the convergence of continued fractions with complex elements, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 2 (1901), 215-233; see also L. Lorentzen and H. Waadeland, Continued Fractions, Volume 1: Convergence Theory, 2nd edition, Atlantis Press, 2008
source.note: Steps 1 to 3 and 5 are written out here; step 4, the convergence for a divergent sum, is the part that the cited work proves.

statement: Let $G$ be a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center. Then $G$ has a [discrete series representation](c:discrete-series-representation) if and only if $G$ has a compact [Cartan subgroup](c:cartan-subgroup), that is, if and only if $\operatorname{rank} G = \operatorname{rank} K$ for a maximal compact subgroup $K$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a connected [semisimple Lie group](c:semisimple-lie-group) with finite center.

conclusion: A [discrete series representation](c:discrete-series-representation) of $G$ exists exactly when $G$ has a compact [Cartan subgroup](c:cartan-subgroup).

proofs.name: Harish-Chandra's characters
proofs.slogan: Turn the compact Cartan condition into equal ranks, rule out discrete series without it, and build them from characters with it.
proofs.scope: An outline of Harish-Chandra's existence criterion; each analytic step is cited. His parametrization of the discrete series and its character formulas are not proved here.

roles.why: Connectedness, semisimplicity and finite center put $G$ in the class where Harish-Chandra's character theory applies.

steps.slogan: Translate the compact Cartan condition into a condition on ranks.
steps.detail: A compact [Cartan subgroup](c:cartan-subgroup) is a torus of dimension $\operatorname{rank} G$ inside a conjugate of $K$. So one exists exactly when a maximal torus of $K$ has dimension $\operatorname{rank} G$, that is, when $\operatorname{rank} K = \operatorname{rank} G$.

steps.slogan: Describe the discrete series representations through their characters.
steps.detail: A [discrete series representation](c:discrete-series-representation) $\pi$ is irreducible and unitary with square-integrable matrix coefficients. Its character $\Theta_\pi$ is an invariant eigendistribution; by Harish-Chandra's regularity theorem it is a locally integrable function that is analytic on the regular set.

steps.slogan: Show that a group without a compact Cartan subgroup has no discrete series.
steps.detail: The cited papers combine the last step with Harish-Chandra's analysis of the character on each Cartan subgroup. Square integrability forces a compact Cartan subgroup to exist. The argument is long, so it is cited and not repeated.

steps.slogan: Build discrete series from regular characters of a compact Cartan subgroup.
steps.detail: Let $T$ be a compact Cartan subgroup and $\lambda$ a regular character of $T$. A Weyl-type quotient on $T$ extends to an invariant eigendistribution $\Theta_\lambda$ on $G$ (part I), and $\pm\Theta_\lambda$ is the character of a discrete series representation (part II). This is cited.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: A discrete series representation forces a compact Cartan subgroup by the necessity step, and a compact Cartan subgroup gives one by the construction. By the first step this is the condition $\operatorname{rank} G = \operatorname{rank} K$.

concepts.c:semisimple-lie-group: Harish-Chandra's character theory is developed for this class of groups.
concepts.c:discrete-series-representation: Its square-integrable matrix coefficients are the property that the proof uses and builds.
concepts.c:cartan-subgroup: A compact Cartan subgroup is the object whose existence the theorem decides.

source.ref: Harish-Chandra, Discrete series for semisimple Lie groups I. Construction of invariant eigendistributions, Acta Mathematica 113 (1965), 241-318, and II. Explicit determination of the characters, Acta Mathematica 116 (1966), 1-111
source.note: Steps 1 and 2 and the joining step are written out here; the necessity and construction steps are the content of the cited papers.

statement: Let $F$ be a [voting system](c:voting-system) that picks a nonempty set of winners from the strict rankings of finitely many voters over at least three alternatives. If each alternative is the sole winner in some profile, and neither an optimist nor a pessimist gains by a false report, then some voter's top choice is always a winner.

hypotheses.text: There are at least three alternatives and finitely many voters, and each voter ranks all alternatives strictly.
The [voting system](c:voting-system) $F$ gives a nonempty set of winners $F(P)$ for every profile $P$ of rankings.
For every alternative $a$ some profile $P$ has $F(P) = \{a\}$.
No voter can improve the best winner, in the voter's own ranking, by reporting a false ranking.
No voter can improve the worst winner, in the voter's own ranking, by reporting a false ranking.

conclusion: Some voter $d$, a weak dictator, has a top choice that lies in $F(P)$ for every profile $P$.

proofs.name: Monotonicity and a pivotal voter
proofs.slogan: Derive monotonicity of sole winners from the two no-gain conditions, then find a weak dictator as in the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem.
proofs.scope: The weak-dictator form of the Duggan-Schwartz theorem, due to Taylor; the original paper words the statement differently. An outline: the first three steps are proved here and the last step is cited.

roles.why: Three alternatives let the cited argument compare two alternatives with a third; for two alternatives majority rule is a counterexample.
A nonempty set of winners makes the best and the worst winner of a voter well defined.
Sole winners exist for every alternative, which starts the unanimity argument.
It keeps the best option of each voter among the winners and keeps a rising sole winner in the winner set.
It removes every other alternative from the winner set when a sole winner rises.

steps.slogan: Show that each voter's best option is always a winner.
steps.detail: Fix voter $i$ and the rankings $P_{-i}$ of the others. Let $O_i$ be the set of all winners that $i$ can reach by some report. The optimist condition gives that the best member of $O_i$ in the true ranking of $i$ lies in $F(P)$.

steps.slogan: Show that a sole winner stays the sole winner when it rises in a ranking.
steps.detail: Let $F(P) = \{a\}$, and let voter $i$ change the ranking so that the set of alternatives below $a$ does not shrink. The optimist condition keeps $a$ among the winners and puts every winner at or below $a$. The pessimist condition then removes every other winner.

steps.slogan: Show that a unanimous top choice is the sole winner.
steps.detail: Some profile has $F = \{x\}$ because $F$ is onto. Move $x$ to the top of every ranking, one voter at a time. By the monotonicity step $F$ stays $\{x\}$, so $F(P) = \{x\}$ whenever all voters rank $x$ first.

steps.slogan: Find the voter whose top choice is always a winner.
steps.detail: The cited paper combines the three facts with an argument of the kind used for the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem. It shows that one voter $d$ has a top choice in $F(P)$ for every $P$. This case analysis is long and is cited here.

concepts.c:voting-system: The system is a rule from rankings to a nonempty set of winners.

source.ref: J. Duggan and T. Schwartz, Strategic manipulability without resoluteness or shared beliefs: Gibbard-Satterthwaite generalized, Social Choice and Welfare 17 (2000), 85-93; weak-dictator form: A. D. Taylor, The manipulability of voting systems, American Mathematical Monthly 109 (2002), 321-337
source.note: Steps 1 to 3 are written out here; step 4 is the dictatorship argument of the cited work.

statement: For nonnegative integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$, the [constant term](c:constant-term) of the [Laurent polynomial](c:laurent-polynomial) $\prod_{i \ne j} (1 - x_i/x_j)^{a_i}$ equals the [multinomial coefficient](c:multinomial-coefficient) $\dfrac{(a_1 + \cdots + a_n)!}{a_1! \cdots a_n!}$.

hypotheses.text: The exponents $a_1, \dots, a_n$ are nonnegative integers.
The symbols $x_1, \dots, x_n$ are independent commuting variables, with $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: The [constant term](c:constant-term) of $\prod_{i \ne j} (1 - x_i/x_j)^{a_i}$ is $(a_1 + \cdots + a_n)!/(a_1! \cdots a_n!)$.

proofs.name: Good's recurrence
proofs.slogan: Show that the constant terms satisfy the multinomial recurrence and boundary values, then compare by induction.
proofs.scope: All $n \ge 1$ and all nonnegative exponents, by induction on $n$ and on $a_1 + \cdots + a_n$. The $q$-analogue and Macdonald's generalization belong to the same family and are not proved here.

roles.why: Nonnegative exponents make each product a Laurent polynomial and give an induction on the exponent sum.
Independent variables are distinct interpolation nodes, so the Lagrange identity holds.

steps.slogan: Prove the identity $\sum_i \prod_{j \ne i} (1 - x_i/x_j)^{-1} = 1$.
steps.detail: Interpolate the constant polynomial $1$ at the distinct nodes $x_1, \dots, x_n$ and evaluate at $0$: $1 = \sum_i \prod_{j \ne i} \frac{-x_j}{x_i - x_j}$. Each factor equals $(1 - x_i/x_j)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Split the product into $n$ products with one exponent lowered.
steps.detail: Write $F_a = \prod_{i \ne j} (1 - x_i/x_j)^{a_i}$ and let all $a_i \ge 1$. Multiply $F_a$ by the identity of the last step. Since $F_{a - e_i} = F_a \prod_{j \ne i}(1 - x_i/x_j)^{-1}$, we get $F_a = \sum_i F_{a - e_i}$, a sum of Laurent polynomials.

steps.slogan: Take constant terms to get the Pascal recurrence.
steps.detail: The [constant term](c:constant-term) is linear on Laurent polynomials. So $C(a) = \sum_i C(a - e_i)$ when all $a_i \ge 1$, where $C(a) = \operatorname{CT} F_a$. The [multinomial coefficients](c:multinomial-coefficient) $M(a)$ obey the same recurrence by Pascal's rule.

steps.slogan: Remove a variable whose exponent is zero.
steps.detail: If $a_k = 0$, the variable $x_k$ occurs in $F_a$ only in factors $(1 - x_i/x_k)^{a_i}$, which are polynomials in $x_k^{-1}$ with constant term $1$. So $C(a) = C(a')$, where $a'$ omits $a_k$; also $M(a) = M(a')$.

steps.slogan: Compare $C$ and $M$ by induction on $n$ and on the exponent sum.
steps.detail: For $n = 1$ both equal $1$. If some $a_k = 0$ and $n \ge 2$, the boundary step reduces $n$. If all $a_i \ge 1$, the recurrence reduces the exponent sum. So $C(a) = M(a)$ for all $a$.

concepts.c:constant-term: The theorem is about this coefficient, and taking it turns the identity into a recurrence.
concepts.c:laurent-polynomial: Each product is a Laurent polynomial, so its constant term is defined and linear.
concepts.c:multinomial-coefficient: The target values obey the same recurrence and boundary values as the constant terms.

source.note: Good's short proof of the conjecture of Dyson, as in I. J. Good, Short proof of a conjecture by Dyson, Journal of Mathematical Physics 11 (1970), 1884; the conjecture was first proved by Wilson and by Gunson in 1962.

statement: Let $G$ be a [compact group](c:compact-group) acting continuously on a [normal space](c:normal-space) $X$, let $A \subseteq X$ be closed and $G$-invariant, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real representation of $G$. Every continuous [equivariant map](c:equivariant-map) $A \to V$ extends to a continuous equivariant map $X \to V$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a compact Hausdorff [group](c:compact-group) that acts continuously on $X$.
$X$ is a [normal space](c:normal-space), and $A \subseteq X$ is closed and $G$-invariant.
$V = \mathbb{R}^m$ carries a continuous linear action of $G$.
The map $f \colon A \to V$ is continuous and [equivariant](c:equivariant-map).

conclusion: There is a continuous equivariant map $\tilde f \colon X \to V$ with $\tilde f|_A = f$.

proofs.name: Tietze extension and averaging
proofs.slogan: Extend by Tietze's theorem while ignoring the action, then average the extension over the group with Haar measure.
proofs.scope: Targets that are finite-dimensional linear representations; other targets, such as retracts of representations, are not covered here. The proof uses the Haar probability measure of $G$, which is invariant on both sides.

roles.why: Compactness gives a Haar probability measure and makes the average continuous in $x$.
Normality and closedness of $A$ allow the Tietze extension; invariance of $A$ lets the average keep $f$ on $A$.
The linear action on $V$ lets $g^{-1}$ act on values, so the average lies in $V$.
Equivariance of $f$ makes each translated value on $A$ equal $f(a)$.

steps.slogan: Extend $f$ to a continuous map on $X$ and ignore the action.
steps.detail: Apply the Tietze extension theorem to each of the $m$ coordinate functions of $f$ on the closed set $A$ of the [normal space](c:normal-space) $X$. This gives a continuous $h \colon X \to V$ with $h|_A = f$. It need not be equivariant.

steps.slogan: Average the translated extension over the group.
steps.detail: Define $\tilde f(x) = \int_G g^{-1} \cdot h(gx)\, dg$, where $dg$ is the [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) of total mass $1$ and $g^{-1}\cdot$ is the linear action on $V$. The integrand is a continuous $V$-valued function on $G \times X$.

steps.slogan: Show that the average depends continuously on $x$.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi(g, x) = g^{-1} h(gx)$. For $x_0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, compactness of $G$ gives a neighborhood $W$ of $x_0$ with $|\varphi(g, x) - \varphi(g, x_0)| < \varepsilon$ for all $g \in G$ and $x \in W$. Integrating gives $|\tilde f(x) - \tilde f(x_0)| \le \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Show that the average is equivariant by invariance of Haar measure.
steps.detail: For $k \in G$, $\tilde f(kx) = \int_G g^{-1} h(gkx)\, dg$. Substitute $g' = gk$, which preserves Haar measure of the compact group. The integral becomes $\int_G k\, g'^{-1} h(g'x)\, dg' = k\, \tilde f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the average equals $f$ on $A$.
steps.detail: Let $a \in A$ and $g \in G$. Then $ga \in A$, so $h(ga) = f(ga) = g f(a)$ by equivariance. Hence $g^{-1} h(ga) = f(a)$ for every $g$, and $\tilde f(a) = \int_G f(a)\, dg = f(a)$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three properties of $\tilde f$.
steps.detail: The map $\tilde f$ is continuous, equivariant, and equal to $f$ on $A$. So it is the required equivariant extension of $f$ to $X$.

concepts.c:compact-group: Compactness gives a Haar probability measure over which the extension is averaged.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality is the hypothesis of the Tietze extension theorem used first.
concepts.c:equivariant-map: The averaged map must commute with the action, and so must $f$.
concepts.c:haar-measure: Its invariance under translation makes the average equivariant.

source.note: The averaging argument for compact transformation groups, as in Bredon, Introduction to Compact Transformation Groups (1972).
